title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Officials gather privately on data centers while residents protest outside in Dorr Twp.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Yesterday's closed-door seminar in Dorr Township drew over a hundred local leaders but also dozens of protesters, and that's our big story tonight.
Graham, this feels like a flashpoint. What exactly happened in Dorr Township yesterday?
More than a hundred municipal officials from Allegan, Barry, and Kent counties met for an invite-only session on zoning and inspections hosted by a private firm.
And outside?
Dozens of residents protested over water use concerns tied to a Microsoft proposal that's under moratorium until 2027.
Why does a closed session like that raise so many alarms for people living nearby?
Residents thirty miles away are already worried their electric bills and water supplies could take a hit if these projects move forward without more public input.
How does this fit into the bigger pattern we've seen across the state lately?
Small towns are becoming test cases. Places like Decatur, Ypsilanti, and Lyon Township are all wrestling with the same questions about power grid strain and who pays for upgrades.
Walk me through the history here. Has Michigan seen this kind of pushback before?
Data center proposals have been accelerating, and communities are looking back at earlier builds that brought jobs but also new power lines and traffic.
What are the main players in these deals?
Big tech companies like Microsoft, local developers, and township boards are at the table, while residents and environmental groups are pushing for more transparency.
Let's talk stakes. How could one of these campuses affect electric bills for regular households?
New facilities can add thousands of megawatts of demand. Utilities have said upgrades might be needed, and the question is whether ratepayers foot part of that bill.
Water is another big one, right?
Cooling systems at large sites can pull significant amounts, and in areas already watching drought patterns that raises red flags for nearby farms and homes.
Farmland conversion is happening too. What does that mean for towns long-term?
Projects like the one nicknamed The Barn in Saline Township are turning agricultural land into industrial sites, shifting tax bases and changing the character of rural communities.
Supporters always mention jobs. How do those promises stack up against the concerns?
Proponents point to construction and operations roles, but critics worry the economic benefits may not offset higher utility costs for everyone else in the area.
What happens next after yesterday's seminar and protests?
More townships are scheduling hearings, and calls for statewide pauses are growing louder from figures like Mike Rogers.
How might this closed-door approach change how future meetings are handled?
Residents are demanding open sessions, and some councils are already considering moratoriums to buy time for better rules.
Is there a sense that this could spread to more counties?
Absolutely. The Dorr example is being watched closely by places like Detroit and Ypsilanti that are weighing their own freezes.
Any sense of what a typical resident should watch for in their own backyard?
Look for notices about zoning changes or utility filings, because those often signal when a project is moving from proposal to construction.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to quick hits.
In Decatur today, neighbors clashed over a proposed campus, worrying about taxes, noise, and power grid impacts while supporters highlighted jobs.
That sounds like the same tension we just discussed. How is Decatur handling it differently?
It's shaping up as an early test case for other small towns, with residents pushing for more details on utility bill effects.
Over in Detroit, environmental groups are calling for a freeze on new projects while the city writes power and water rules.
Right, they say hyperscale builds could strain the grid and raise household costs, and a moratorium would let officials assess the real impacts.
Mike Rogers is pushing a statewide pause until utilities prove they can handle the load without rate hikes.
He targeted projects that could add thousands of megawatts, noting voters from both parties are concerned about who pays.
Ypsilanti is debating a year-long halt at tonight's council meeting.
Residents there fear spikes in electricity rates and water strain, and the pause would give time to craft permanent zoning rules.
Vice-presidential candidate Vance stopped in Sterling Heights and tied data centers to both jobs and power bill risks.
He referenced University of Michigan research and noted how new facilities could affect household costs across the state.
Yesterday also saw a closed-door pitch that raised electric bill and water fears for residents thirty miles away.
Demonstrators rallied outside while officials heard the presentations, leaving many locals questioning whose voices are shaping the deals.
In Lyon Township, the developer faces another hearing next month amid worries about grid and roads.
Residents there have already flagged power demand and construction impacts on local infrastructure.
Near Ann Arbor, a big AI facility hit a million construction hours, and Washtenaw County residents are watching rate and water effects.
Jobs are growing, but so are questions about long-term taxpayer costs once it ramps up.
And in Saline Township, The Barn project is rising fast on farmland.
Nearby residents will see new power lines and traffic, plus potential tax shifts as the facility comes online.
On deck for listeners, Ypsilanti council meets tonight on that proposed moratorium.
No other major public meetings are listed for tomorrow, but township agendas can change quickly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Closed-Door Data Center Talks Spark Protests in West Michigan
